stem: Reyansh builds an $n$-by-$n$ square of unit tiles. He peels it into $n$ nested L-shaped layers: the outermost L uses $2n-1$ tiles, then $2n-3$, and so on down to $1$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly explains why the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equals $n^{2}$?

options.text: The $n$-by-$n$ square partitions into those $n$ nested odd L-layers, so $1+3+\cdots+(2n-1)=n^{2}$.
Any collection of odd numbers sums to a square, even when the odds are not the first $n$ consecutive odds from $1$.
The same L-layer story also forces the up-and-down sum of ordinary counting numbers to equal $n^{2}$.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

part_answers.answer: An $n$-by-$n$ square splits into $n$ nested L-layers whose sizes are the first $n$ odd numbers, so their total is $n^{2}$.

teacher.key_rationale: The square's area equals the sum of those odd L-layers. Skipping the consecutive-from-1 condition, or extending the story to the counting-number sum, misses that hinge.
